title: Three steps in
hookLine: many step back and then forward before beginning, as if approaching a king

cards: A pause in the doorway of a boss's office before you step in. People mark entrances even when nothing stands in the way.
Before the Amidah, many Jews make one with their feet: three small steps backward, then three small steps forward, ending exactly where they started.
If you didn't know, you'd think they'd forgotten something and changed their mind.
But it's a whole entrance, compressed into six steps on a carpet, and it borrows its shape from the way people once walked into a throne room.

teach.b: The steps forward are the older idea. Before you speak to a king, you approach. Commentators point to three moments in the Bible where someone draws near before speaking to God or to power.
Abraham draws near to plead for Sodom. Judah draws near to Joseph, the ruler of Egypt, to plead for his brother. Elijah draws near on Mount Carmel before he prays.
In the old Jewish translation, Genesis says simply: "And Abraham drew near." Three nearings, three steps. The step backward first is a later custom, and not everyone does it.

The idea: you can't walk forward into a presence you're already standing in, so you make a little room, step back, and then come in properly. Halachic codes record the forward steps as a custom many keep.
At the end of the Amidah there are three steps back again: the Talmud, in Yoma 53b, compares it to a student taking leave of a teacher, backing away rather than turning around.

teach.h: THREE STEPS IN, THREE STEPS OUT.
teach.b: So the whole prayer sits inside a doorway: three steps in, three steps out. Prayer doesn't begin when the words begin. It begins when you decide to go in.
Before the steps, you're in your day. After them, you're somewhere else, in front of someone. Same carpet.

how: Many Jews take three small steps forward before beginning the Amidah, often stepping back first to make room, and at the end take three steps back and bow to each side before stepping forward again; customs on the opening steps vary between communities.

games.q: you're about to begin the Amidah, already standing in your place. what do many people do first?
o: take three steps forward, often after stepping back.
sit down and wait for the leader.
games.why: many step back to make room, then three steps forward: approaching, as if before a king.

practice: If you can stand, try it now: three small steps back, a pause, then three small steps forward; if not, take them in your mind.
Stay where you've landed for a few breaths, and notice whether the same spot feels like a different room.

wordCard.voice: Drew near. Abraham, before pleading for Sodom; Judah, before Joseph; Elijah, before he prayed — the model for the three steps taken into the Amidah.

carryVoice: Your line: same carpet, different room. The week walked from the Shema's last paragraphs, through true and firm and the sea, to no gap, the standing prayer and its doorway. That's day five hundred seventy-four.
